clue.text: Big type, apparently of supreme excellence

explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' softens the second sense, since the word is a noun for a perfect example rather than an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Paragon is an old printers' name for a large size of type, and a paragon is also a model of perfection.

clue.text: Macaulay's contribution to gamesmanship?

parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote a satirical novel whose title looks like a doctrine named after Stephen Potter, author of Gamesmanship

explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Potter wrote 'Gamesmanship'; Rose Macaulay's 1920 novel title reads as if it were his creed, though it predates him.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Macaulay's novel title looks like a philosophy named after the Gamesmanship author.

clue.text: Give Dr a remarkably holy book

indicators.note: remarkably suggests the letters of the preceding words are arranged in a striking new way

explanation.surface: A request to hand a doctor some unusually sacred text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkably' rearranges GIVE, DR and A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rig Veda is the oldest collection of Hindu sacred hymns, a scripture.

clue.text: It's a small world " for this man's priest

definitions.text: It's a small world " for this man's priest

parts.words: It's a small world " for this man's priest
parts.note: the Italian writer's priest Don Camillo lives in a 'Little World', a small Po valley village

explanation.surface: A remark that the world is small, applied to a writer's clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Giovannino Guareschi's stories are 'The Little World of Don Camillo', about a village priest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian humorist created Don Camillo, priest of the 'Little World' stories.

clue.text: Free wheeling American poet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Free wheeling' looks like a description of a carefree American; it points to the Nash car.
explanation.definitionFit: Nash was an American motor manufacturer whose cars offered freewheeling, and Ogden Nash was a comic poet.

clue.text: One of Williams's signs of loss

definitions.text: One of Williams's signs of loss

parts.words: One of Williams's signs of loss
parts.note: Hugo Williams's first poetry collection is titled '... of Loss'; one sign is a single item from that title

explanation.surface: A single indicator of grief as described by a poet called Williams.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugo Williams's 1965 collection 'Symptoms of Loss' supplies the plural; the clue asks for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign of an illness or condition is its indicator, as in the book title.

clue.text: Fruitful upland scene of Walpole's Gothic revivalism

definitions.text: Fruitful upland scene of Walpole's Gothic revivalism

parts.words: Fruitful upland scene of Walpole's Gothic revivalism
parts.note: fruitful upland is a hill named after a soft red fruit, the house Horace Walpole built in Gothic style at Twickenham

explanation.surface: A productive hillside where Walpole pioneered the Gothic style.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace Walpole's villa Strawberry Hill launched the Gothic revival; 'fruitful' gives the fruit and 'upland' the Hill, which is not entered.
explanation.definitionFit: Strawberry Hill is Walpole's Gothic villa, so the fruit word names that scene.

clue.text: Historical novelist in secret society?

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second sense: a Freemason is in that society.
explanation.definitionFit: A. E. W. Mason wrote historical romances, and a member of the Freemasons belongs to a secretive fraternity.

clue.text: "With their — hats they looked very much like Knaves of Spades" (M. J. Higgins, Essays on Social Subjects)

definitions.text: "With their — hats they looked very much like Knaves of Spades" (M. J. Higgins, Essays on Social Subjects)

parts.words: "With their — hats they looked very much like Knaves of Spades" (M. J. Higgins, Essays on Social Subjects)
parts.note: the missing word is the three-cornered style of hat worn by the playing-card knaves

explanation.surface: A Victorian essayist compares people in distinctive hats to playing-card knaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-cornered hat, as the knaves on playing cards wear, fills the gap.

clue.text: Go back to little review for big man

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a review cut short

indicators.note: back tells us the word go is turned round

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to return to a minor magazine to find a giant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the clue's first word round, and 'to' sets it after the short word for a magazine; 'big man' is the legendary giant.
explanation.definitionFit: Magog is one of the legendary giants Gog and Magog, guardians of London.

clue.text: Arcadian city, for example, found in shrub

indicators.note: found in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the tea plant is an evergreen shrub

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek town, cited as an instance, discovered inside a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' places the abbreviation inside the drink's plant; 'shrub' hides the tea bush behind a garden word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tegea was an ancient city of Arcadia in the Peloponnese.

clue.text: Essential ingredient of Sturm und Drang?

definitions.text: Essential ingredient of Sturm und Drang?

parts.words: Essential ingredient of Sturm und Drang?
parts.note: the German movement's name translates as storm and stress, so putting emphasis is part of it

explanation.surface: Asking what lies at the heart of the German Romantic movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Sturm und Drang is 'storm and stress'; the answer also means emphasising, the essence of drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is half the movement's English name, so laying stress is its ingredient.

clue.text: Harry the king, Bedford and—

parts.note: a line from Henry V's St Crispin's Day speech listing the nobles, completed by a duke's title

explanation.surface: A list of medieval nobles left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Henry V: 'Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot...'; the duke shares a name with a Devon city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Exeter completes Henry V's roll call of familiar names.

clue.text: Galsworthy's final work

parts.note: the last novel of the Forsyte trilogy A Modern Comedy, and a phrase for any artist's farewell piece

explanation.surface: The last book of an Edwardian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Galsworthy's 1928 novel of that title ends the second Forsyte trilogy; it was not literally his last book.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell performance or last creation is so called, from the dying bird's legendary song.

clue.text: Yearn over senior student known as narrative poet

parts.note: to yearn is to long
a fellow is a senior member of a college

explanation.surface: Longing to outrank a senior scholar known for verse.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' just places LONG above FELLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote long story poems such as Hiawatha and Evangeline.

clue.text: Is a current form of Scott's usurer

parts.note: taken as written
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: A remark on a modern version of a character in Walter Scott.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac of York is the Jewish moneylender in Scott's Ivanhoe.

clue.text: Tyndale was concerned with that of a "Christen man"

definitions.text: Tyndale was concerned with that of a "Christen man"

parts.words: Tyndale was concerned with that of a "Christen man"
parts.note: William Tyndale's 1528 treatise is titled The ___ of a Christen Man, on submission to authority

explanation.surface: The Bible translator's worry about a Christian's duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyndale's tract argued for the dutiful submission of subjects to their king.

clue.text: Vain Eliot possibly sacrosanct…

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters could form something else

explanation.surface: Perhaps a conceited poet thought himself beyond criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges VAIN ELIOT; the dots link to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untouchable and safe from violation is sacrosanct.

clue.text: … using characters from Tom Brown and The Horse's Mouth in Somerset village quartet

parts.note: East is Tom's friend in Tom Brown's Schooldays
Coker is the barmaid in Joyce Cary's The Horse's Mouth

explanation.surface: Borrowing people from two novels to set a poem in a West Country village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters from' covers both books. The definition names the village and the Four Quartets poem named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: East Coker is a Somerset village and the second of T. S. Eliot's Four Quartets, following the previous clue's Eliot.

clue.text: Dramatist heard a cantor at service

indicators.note: heard says the phrase is spoken aloud

parts.note: a cantor sings at Mass, so he is a Mass singer

explanation.surface: A playwright listened to a church singer during worship.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Massinger was a Jacobean playwright, author of A New Way to Pay Old Debts.

clue.text: Composer encountered in corpore sana

indicators.note: Latin for in the body, so a piece goes inside the next word

parts.note: to have encountered someone is to have met them

explanation.surface: A musician found within a healthy body, after Juvenal's motto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in corpore' (Latin, in the body) is the container signal, playing on Juvenal's 'mens sana in corpore sano'; the Latin 'sana' supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedřich Smetana was the Czech composer of Má vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: Sirens indicate five current units

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
amps measure electric current

explanation.surface: Seductive women signal a measure of electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Vamps are seductive women who lure men, as the sirens of myth did.

clue.text: Military music with measure of folk stories

parts.note: a march is music for soldiers
an en is a printer's measure of width

explanation.surface: Soldiers' tunes accompanying traditional tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Märchen is the German word for fairy tales and folk tales.

clue.text: "Bear up the helm-—! Rodmond cries" (William Falconer)

definitions.text: "Bear up the helm-—! Rodmond cries" (William Falconer)

parts.words: "Bear up the helm-—! Rodmond cries" (William Falconer)
parts.note: from Falconer's poem The Shipwreck; the missing nautical word means toward the windward side

explanation.surface: A seaman's command from an 18th-century poem of shipwreck.
explanation.definitionFit: The helm is put toward the wind's side, the windward, a sailing order.

clue.text: King Death has these ears, thought Thomas Lovell Beddoes

definitions.text: King Death has these ears, thought Thomas Lovell Beddoes

parts.words: King Death has these ears, thought Thomas Lovell Beddoes
parts.note: Beddoes, in Death's Jest-Book, gives Death donkey ears, as Midas had

explanation.surface: A Romantic poet imagines the shape of Death's ears.
explanation.definitionFit: Donkeys' long ears were Midas's punishment, and Beddoes gives them to Death.

clue.text: Part of the Irish literary tradition belongs to them

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A piece of Ireland's writing heritage claimed by some group.
explanation.definitionFit: Something belonging to them is described with this possessive word.

clue.text: Go to doctor in charge to find reclusive hymnodist

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A trip to the doctor reveals a hermit who wrote hymns.
explanation.definitionFit: St Godric of Finchale was a medieval hermit whose hymns are among the earliest English songs.

clue.text: Night's many seers, according to Woolrich

definitions.text: Night's many seers, according to Woolrich

parts.words: Night's many seers, according to Woolrich
parts.note: Cornell Woolrich's novel says night has a thousand of these watchers

explanation.surface: A thriller writer's view of what sees in the dark.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolrich's novel Night Has a Thousand Eyes names the organs of sight.

clue.text: Possibly staple Gay drama

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Perhaps John Gay's standard fare was theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges STAPLE GAY; John Gay wrote The Beggar's Opera.
explanation.definitionFit: A play written for the theatre is a piece of drama.

clue.text: Scene of Ahab's victory in an ingenious trap he knew of

indicators.note: in signals the answer lies within the run of clue words that follows

explanation.surface: A biblical battle site captured by a clever ambush someone knew of.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across trAP HE Knew.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahab defeated the Syrians under Ben-hadad at Aphek, as in 1 Kings 20.

clue.text: She fell for Smith

parts.note: a small bird, female in the clue, whose fall is noted in the Gospel and in Stevie Smith's verse

explanation.surface: A woman who was smitten with a man named Smith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell for' suggests love, but means dropping dead, as in 'the fall of a sparrow'.
explanation.definitionFit: The small brown bird whose fall Providence notes appears in Stevie Smith's poems.

clue.text: He received the Pulitzer Prize from a restful position

definitions.text: He received the Pulitzer Prize from a restful position

parts.words: He received the Pulitzer Prize from a restful position
parts.note: the restful position is the angle of repose, title of the American novelist's 1972 prize-winning novel

explanation.surface: A prize-winner who accepted his award lying down.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallace Stegner won the 1972 Pulitzer for 'Angle of Repose', a restful position.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallace Stegner's Angle of Repose won him the fiction Pulitzer.
